title: Control of Structure and Epitaxy of High-k Metal Oxides Through In Situ Electron Microscopy
content: Engineering new dielectrics for microelectronics has been a major focus of the semiconductor industry as scaling device dimensions runs into limits of traditionally dominant SiO2 gate dielectrics like SiO2 [1]. Attention has therefore turned to transition metal oxides such as hafnia (HfO2). Amorphous hafnia formed via atomic layer deposition (ALD) enabled a critical step forward in the reduction of transistor dimensions by introducing a high-k dielectric to silicon electronics [2]. Further opportunities are anticipated through the use of crystalline hafnia-based dielectrics. Crystalline layers are formed by annealing the initially amorphous ALD layer, and the resulting ferroelectric properties and improvements in dielectric capacitance make these crystalline dielectrics particularly exciting for next-generation devices [3, 4]. However, now that 2D materials are proposed as channel materials, required at these new frontiers of ultrathin vertical dimensions, a challenge of the ALD process has become evident: ALD does not readily form a uniform layer on the chemically inert 2D surface [5, 6]. One promising strategy is the use of an intermediate metal seed layer deposited via physical vapor deposition (PVD) which has been shown to improve ALD film uniformity [7]. In this work, we explore the formation of crystalline metal oxides, aiming to achieve the high quality epitaxy and phase control on 2D materials that would be required in microelectronic device design that incorporates ferroelectric behavior to improve performance and explore novel device functionality. We use environmental transmission electron microscopy (ETEM) to study the formation of crystalline dielectric domains from amorphous ALD oxides using in situ heating in gas environments, as well as ultra-high vacuum transmission electron microscopy (UHVTEM) to quantify the crystalline oxides that result from PVD of thin metal films.
